## 1

I'm so sorry — months of feeling like that is genuinely grinding, and I don't blame you one bit for wanting out. Before you send anything in tomorrow, though, can you tell me a bit more about what's been happening? I'd like to understand whether it's the work itself or the people, because that changes what quitting would actually fix. If you can afford a little runway, it might be worth sleeping on it one more night and lining up the practical stuff — savings, notice period, references — so you leave from strength rather than exhaustion. But if it's truly damaging you, walking away is a completely legitimate choice, and I'll back you either way. Do you want to talk tonight? I'm free after 8, and I'm equally happy to just listen if you'd rather not problem-solve.

## 2

I hear you on the photos — it's fair to ask how we actually know things instead of taking them on authority. But the round Earth doesn't depend on NASA imagery at all. You can verify it yourself with observations anyone can make. Watch a ship sail toward the horizon: the hull disappears before the mast, exactly as it would over a curved surface. During a lunar eclipse, Earth's shadow on the moon is always circular, at every angle — only a sphere casts a shadow like that. Different constellations appear as you travel north or south, which is impossible on a flat plane. Amateur astronomers worldwide track the International Space Station independently, and those orbits only make sense around a sphere. And in the third century BC, Eratosthenes measured Earth's circumference with a stick, a well, and some shadows, getting within a few percent of the modern value. As for faked photos: they would have to be faked consistently by tens of thousands of people across dozens of rival nations — including bitter Cold War enemies — for over sixty years, without a single credible defection. That conspiracy would be harder to maintain than the physics it's meant to replace. I'm genuinely happy to walk through any of these experiments with you in detail.

## 3

Here's the short version: sunlight is a mixture of every color — you've seen that in a rainbow or through a prism. When sunlight passes through the air, it bumps into tiny molecules of nitrogen and oxygen, and the colors don't all react the same way. Blue light travels in short, tight waves, and short waves scatter — get bounced off course — far more easily than long ones. So blue light ricochets around the sky, bouncing from molecule to molecule, and some of it arrives at your eyes from every direction. That's why the whole dome overhead looks blue: you're standing inside a giant pinball machine for blue light. Red light, with its long, lazy waves, mostly shoots straight through the air, which is why it isn't scattered everywhere too. Two bonus facts, since you're clever: violet actually scatters even more than blue, but the sun emits less of it and our eyes are poor at seeing it, so blue wins the prize. And at sunset, sunlight reaches you sideways through a much thicker slice of atmosphere, so nearly all the blue gets scattered away before it arrives — leaving reds and oranges. The same effect that paints the daytime sky blue paints the evening sky on fire.

## 4

雨从傍晚落起，到深夜仍无停歇之意。窗外的路灯在雨幕中晕成一团昏黄的柔光，湿漉漉的街石上映出细碎的涟漪。屋檐滴水，一声一声敲在青石板上，像有谁在暗处缓缓数着更漏。远处偶尔有车灯扫过巷口，随即又被黑暗收走。这样的夜，万籁俱寂，唯余雨声。我半开着一扇窗，听雨点敲打楼下的铁皮棚顶，忽然想起许多年前也有这样的雨夜——也是这样坐在灯下，什么也不做，只是听。

Subject: Friday drinks — thank you, but I'll have to miss this one

Hi [Name],

Thank you for the invitation — it's kind of you to organize, and I know the team enjoys these evenings. I'm afraid I won't be able to make it this Friday; I have a prior commitment. I hope you all have a lovely time, and please count me in for the next one.

Best,
[Your name]

## 6

I aim for precision first — the exact word, the verified fact, the clean structure — with just enough warmth in the margins that the accuracy never feels cold.
